5.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Perthes Disease: Pathology & Classification
5.1.b:
Perthes disease is the hip disease of the small, active boy, and the one that heals itself, well or badly.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is Perthes disease?"
- "**Idiopathic avascular necrosis** of the capital femoral epiphysis in a child."
- "A boy of **4–8 years**, with a limp; bilateral in about **10%**."
- "It heals by itself; the outcome depends on the **shape** in which it heals."

### Definition
The definition is short, and every word in it excludes something.
- **Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease (LCPD)**: idiopathic osteonecrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis
- Necrosis is followed by revascularisation, resorption and new bone: a **self-repairing** process
- Adult AVN (avascular necrosis) progresses to collapse and arthritis; Perthes may heal round

#### What Perthes Is Not
- AVN with a **known cause** is not Perthes: trauma, infection, tumour, steroids, surgery
- AVN after **SCFE** (slipped capital femoral epiphysis) or DDH treatment is secondary AVN
- Onset after **12 years** is **juvenile AVN**, not Perthes (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

### Names and History
Each old name records one theory or one look of the disease.

| Name | What it records |
|---|---|
| **Legg–Calvé–Perthes** | Legg, Calvé and Perthes described it in **1910** |
| Waldenström | described it a year earlier; his stages carry his name |
| **Coxa plana** | the flat head it leaves |
| Osteochondritis deformans coxae juvenilis | an osteochondrosis deforming the young hip |
| Pseudo-coxalgia | a limp that looks painful, with little pain |
| Legg stress fracture | Legg's post-traumatic theory |

- **Osteochondrosis**: fragmentation of an epiphysis or apophysis
- Its family: Osgood–Schlatter, Sever, Sinding-Larsen–Johansson and Blount disease

### Epidemiology
Picture the patient before the film: a small, very active boy of school age.

| Feature | Typical value |
|---|---|
| Age at onset | **4–8** years; average **7** (Campbell) |
| Sex | boys **3–5×** girls |
| Bilateral | ≈**10%**, rarely at the same stage |
| Bone age | delayed about **2 years** |
| Incidence | higher in Asian, Inuit and Central European children |

- Boys outnumber girls 5:1 (Handbook) or 3:1 (Campbell)
- Bilateral disease is ≈10%; Miller quotes 12–15%
- Other links: family history, low birth weight, abnormal presentation, ADHD
- Children with Perthes look **small for their age**

- Perthes is a small, busy boy of seven who jumps off every sofa: young bones, a fragile blood supply and endless falls.

5.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Perthes Disease: Pathology & Classification
5.2.b:
The cause is unknown, but the sequence after the first ischaemic attack is well understood.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does Perthes develop?"
- "An **unknown first ischaemic attack** kills the cells of the ossific nucleus; the bone architecture stays."
- "Revascularisation lays new bone on dead bone: **increased density**, still silent."
- "A **subchondral fracture** causes pain, and a **second, mechanical** ischaemia makes the head deformable."

### Aetiological Theories
None is proven; know them as a list.

| Theory | Evidence or idea |
|---|---|
| **Vascular, thrombotic** | coagulopathy: low **protein C and S**, thrombophilia (Campbell) |
| Venous | impaired venous drainage, raised intraosseous pressure |
| **Synovitis and effusion** | tamponade of the epiphyseal vessels |
| **Mechanical, traumatic** | hyperactive or heavy child; repeated subchondral injury |
| Hereditary | family history; ethnic clustering |
| Hormonal | low growth hormone and delayed bone age |
| Infective | a preceding viral or bacterial illness |

- Studies for and against a coagulopathy keep the cause **elusive**
- An irritable hip is not proven to cause Perthes

### The Vulnerable Blood Supply
Between 4 and 8 years the epiphysis hangs on one source; hip blood supply → 01 Approach.
[[FIG: Fig 5.1 · 5.2
- The **lateral epiphyseal vessels** from the MFCA (medial femoral circumflex artery) feed the nucleus
- The formed physis blocks the **metaphyseal** vessels
- The **ligamentum teres** artery reaches the head only after **7–8 years** (Handbook)
- So 4–8 years is the window of single supply

### The Normal Growing Epiphysis
Pathology makes sense only against the normal head of a child.
- The ossific nucleus sits inside thick **epiphyseal cartilage**
[[FIG: Fig 5.2 · 5.2
- Articular cartilage covers it, as in the adult
[[FIG: Fig 5.3 · 5.2
- A **germinal cell layer** around the nucleus forms bone, like a second growth plate
[[FIG: Fig 5.4 · 5.2

| Layer | Nourished by | In ischaemia |
|---|---|---|
| Articular cartilage | synovial fluid | keeps growing |
| Epiphyseal cartilage | synovial fluid | keeps growing |
| **Germinal layer** of the nucleus | **epiphyseal arteries** | dies; growth stops |

- No vessel crosses the **physis**, so the nucleus depends on epiphyseal arteries

### The First Ischaemic Attack
The first attack kills cells but leaves the building standing.
- The epiphyseal vessels occlude; the cause is unknown
[[FIG: Fig 5.5 · 5.2
- The germinal layer dies, so the nucleus **stops growing**; it does not shrink
[[FIG: Fig 5.6 · 5.2
- The fluid-fed cartilage keeps growing, so the head keeps its size

#### Relatively Small Nucleus and Wide Joint Space
- The film shows a **smaller ossific nucleus** than the normal side
[[FIG: Fig 5.7 · 5.2
- The **joint space looks wider**: thick growing cartilage, not effusion
- These are the earliest film signs, often incidental

### Revascularisation and Creeping Substitution
The body re-enters the dead nucleus through its intact channels.
- Cells die, but trabeculae, cavities and vascular channels stay intact
[[FIG: Fig 5.8 · 5.2
- Vessels grow in as granulation tissue; osteoclasts resorb dead bone
- **Woven bone** is laid on dead lamellae: **creeping substitution**
[[FIG: Fig 5.9 · 5.2

#### Increased Density
- New bone on dead bone → **increased density** of the nucleus
[[FIG: Fig 5.10 · 5.2
- Up to here the child has **no complaint**: the disease is clinically silent

MEMORY HOOK — the gassed building
- The first attack is gas in a building: the residents die, but stairs and lifts stay, so new tenants move in easily.

### The Subchondral Fracture
The fracture, not the necrosis, makes the child limp.
- Weak woven subchondral bone breaks after a jump or a fall, or spontaneously
- Fracture debris causes synovitis and effusion → **pain and limp**
- So the subchondral fracture marks the **clinical onset**
- It shows best on the **frog-lateral** view: the **crescent sign** (Caffey sign)
[[FIG: Fig 5.11 · 5.2
- It is caught in only ≈**30%**: it appears and disappears early (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- It happens in the dense stage, just before fragmentation

#### Healing Without a Fracture
- With no fracture, the nucleus revascularises and resumes growth silently
- The scar of the old arrest leaves a **head-inside-head** appearance, like a Harris line
[[FIG: Fig 5.12 · 5.2
- Such a child "had Perthes" and nobody knew

### The Second, Mechanical Ischaemic Attack
The fracture strikes a revascularised, weaker epiphysis and demolishes its channels.
- The fracture is a **second ischaemic attack**, mechanical this time
[[FIG: Fig 5.13 · 5.2
- Woven bone is not lamellar, so it cannot resist strain

| Finding | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Dead lamellar bone | the first attack |
| **Dead woven bone** | new bone killed by the fracture |
| **Dead granulation tissue** | new vessels killed |
| Fibrous tissue, cartilage necrosis | repeated injury |

- Articular cartilage may also necrose or turn fibrous over the fracture
[[FIG: Fig 5.14 · 5.2
- These dead new tissues are the **hallmark** of a second attack
[[FIG: Fig 5.15 · 5.2
- Channels are obliterated, so revascularisation is **slow** and patchy
[[FIG: Fig 5.16 · 5.2
- The epiphysis loses structural stability → it can **deform and collapse**

| | First attack | Second attack |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | unknown | **subchondral fracture** |
| Substrate | normal epiphysis | revascularised, weaker epiphysis |
| Channels | intact | obliterated |
| Clinical | silent | pain and limp |
| Result | may reform normally | liable to deformation |

HIGH YIELD — the bulldozer
- The second attack is a bulldozer: it flattens the building, so the new tenants must rebuild from rubble, and the head can be squashed meanwhile.

#### Repeated Attacks
- Perthes is AVN **complicated by a subchondral fracture**, not plain AVN (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Each new fall can add a fracture, a new attack and a longer course
- So a careful, protected child usually has a **shorter** course

5.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Perthes Disease: Pathology & Classification
5.3.b:
The stages are the film's shadow of the pathology just described.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the stages of Perthes?"
- "**Waldenström**: initial (condensation), fragmentation, reossification (healing), healed (remodelling)."
- "The head is **plastic** during fragmentation: the acetabulum moulds it."
- "**Subchondral ossification** means healing has begun: the shape is now fixed."

### Waldenström Stages
Every case passes through four stages over about **2–5 years** (Handbook).
[[FIG: Fig 5.17 · 5.3

| Stage | Duration | Film |
|---|---|---|
| **Initial** (condensation) | a few months | small dense nucleus, wide medial joint space, crescent sign |
| **Fragmentation** | **1–2 years** | patchy lucent and dense areas, collapse, lateral extrusion |
| **Reossification** (healing) | up to **18 months** (Campbell) | new bone fills in; subchondral ossification |
| **Healed** (remodelling) | until skeletal maturity | trabeculae return; final shape |

- Films may stay normal for **3–6 months** after symptoms start (Campbell)
- The stage is a **radiological** description, not a histological one
- A modified scheme splits stages I–III into early (a) and late (b) parts
[[FIG: Fig 5.18 · 5.3

#### Initial Stage
- Possible synovitis; then infarction and **sclerosis** of a smaller nucleus
- Medial joint space widening and the subchondral **crescent sign**

#### Fragmentation Stage
- Resorption of dead bone gives the fragmented look
[[FIG: Fig 5.19 · 5.3
- Symptoms are most marked, and the **lateral pillar** is graded here
- The medial joint space widens: unossified fibrocartilage fills it, not effusion
- The head may **extrude laterally**; metaphyseal cysts and the Gage sign appear
- A fragmented film is not a broken head: cartilage stays smooth at surgery

#### Reossification and Healed Stages
- New bone fills the epiphysis and takes the shape of its cartilage mould
- **Subchondral ossification**: a fine white line under the articular surface
[[FIG: Fig 5.20 · 5.3
- Dots become a line, then a dense rim
[[FIG: Fig 5.21 · 5.3
- Once the line appears, the disease is **healing**, even if fragments persist
[[FIG: Fig 5.22 · 5.3
- The healed head **remodels** until skeletal maturity
[[FIG: Fig 5.23 · 5.3
- A young child may heal round even untreated
[[FIG: Fig 5.24 · 5.3

PITFALL — fragmentation or healing on one film?
- One film cannot always tell them apart; repeat it after **3–6 months**
- Say → "**more lucency means active fragmentation; more density or a subchondral line means healing**"

### Biological Plasticity
The fragmenting head is soft clay, and the acetabulum is its mould.
- During fragmentation the head is **mouldable**: round mould, round head
[[FIG: Fig 5.25 · 5.3
- A subluxed head is bitten by the acetabular edge and deforms
- After subchondral ossification the shape is fixed, so containment is then useless
- Containment treatment → 06 Perthes Treatment

### Deformities of the Healed Head
Each deformity follows a known step of the pathology.

| Deformity | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Coxa plana** | subchondral fracture flattens the head |
| **Coxa magna** | reactive hyperaemia enlarges the head |
| **Mushroom head** | flattening and lateral spread |
| **Coxa breva** | premature physeal closure; short neck |
| **Coxa vara** | larger part of the physis arrested |
| Relative trochanteric overgrowth | head stops, trochanter keeps growing |

#### Each Deformity on the Film
- **Coxa plana**: a flat, depressed head
[[FIG: Fig 5.26 · 5.3
- **Coxa magna**: a healed head larger than the other side
[[FIG: Fig 5.27 · 5.3
- **Mushroom head**: flat and spread beyond the acetabular edge
[[FIG: Fig 5.28 · 5.3
- Complete physeal arrest: a small head on a short neck, **coxa breva**
[[FIG: Fig 5.29 · 5.3
- Arrest of a larger part of the physis tilts the neck into **coxa vara**
[[FIG: Fig 5.30 · 5.3
- **Transphyseal** ossification closes the physis early
- The greater trochanter is not truly overgrown: the neck simply stopped

#### Sagging Rope Sign
- A thin, curved, U-shaped dense line across the proximal metaphysis (Greenspan)
[[FIG: Fig 5.31 · 5.3
- It marks the lower edge of a broad, mushroomed head: advanced Perthes

#### Hinge Abduction
- The extruded lateral head ossifies into a bump
[[FIG: Fig 5.32 · 5.3
- On abduction the bump hinges on the lateral acetabular rim
- So abduction is blocked and the hip sits in **fixed adduction**
- Arthrography shows it before the bump ossifies

MEMORY HOOK — the door hinge
- Hinge abduction is a door with a stone under it: try to open it (abduct) and it only pivots on the stone (the lateral bump).

### Subluxation and Shenton's Line
Subluxation in Perthes means true collapse of the whole head.
- **Subluxation** = a broken **Shenton's line** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 5.33 · 5.3
- In a young child, thick cartilage keeps head height even if the nucleus collapses
[[FIG: Fig 5.34 · 5.3
- In an older child little cartilage is left, so the head itself collapses
- It is a very alarming sign, read on the plain film without MRI

| | Young child | Older child |
|---|---|---|
| Epiphyseal cartilage | abundant | thin |
| Nucleus collapse | head height kept | head collapses |
| Shenton's line | intact | **broken** |

### Metaphyseal Changes
The metaphysis may share the ischaemia.
- **Metaphyseal cysts** and a broad neck appear in severe cases
[[FIG: Fig 5.35 · 5.3
- Their cause is unclear; most likely disordered growth
- They show best on **CT**

### The Acetabulum
The acetabulum follows the head, so do not call it dysplastic.
- A large or flat head moulds the acetabulum to its own shape
[[FIG: Fig 5.36 · 5.3
- This is **not acetabular dysplasia**: no pelvic osteotomy to "cover" it
[[FIG: Fig 5.37 · 5.3
- An affected acetabulum does not suggest TB (tuberculosis) rather than Perthes, as was once taught
[[FIG: Fig 5.38 · 5.3

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does Perthes present?"
- "A boy of **4–8** with a **limp**, often painless at first."
- "Pain in the groin, thigh or **knee**, worse after activity."
- "**Limited abduction and internal rotation**; later a Trendelenburg gait."

### Symptoms
The complaint is mild, so diagnosis is late.
- A **limp**, intermittent and activity-related, sometimes painless: pseudo-coxalgia
- Pain in the groin, thigh or **knee**
- Symptoms last about **6 weeks** before diagnosis (Campbell)
- Ask for trauma, family history and a recent infection

### Signs
Each sign follows the irritable joint first, then the deformed head.

| Sign | Cause |
|---|---|
| Antalgic gait | synovitis after a subchondral fracture |
| **Limited internal rotation** and flexion | raised capsular pressure; impingement |
| **Limited abduction** | adductor spasm; later hinge abduction |
| Flexion deformity (Thomas test) | synovitis; hip held flexed |
| **Drehmann sign** | flexion forces the hip into external rotation |
| **Trendelenburg** sign | high trochanter weakens the abductors |
| Thigh atrophy, mild shortening | disuse; head collapse |

- Leg-length difference is usually small and rarely symptomatic
- Examination signs and photographs → 01 Approach

MEMORY HOOK — the quiet limp
- Perthes limps louder than it hurts: a cheerful boy who limps after football is Perthes until the film says no.

#### Abductor Weakness
- The neck stops growing, the trochanter does not: **supratrochanteric shortening**
- The pelvis dips on the unsupported side when standing on the affected leg
- A trunk lurch can mask it: a false-negative Trendelenburg test
- Bilateral disease gives a **waddling** gait
[[FIG: Fig 5.62 · 5.5

PITFALL — the stiff hip is the warning
- Loss of motion at any time changes the prognosis for the worse (Campbell)
- Say → "**I measure abduction and internal rotation at every visit**"

### Plain Radiographs
The film shows the stage, the severity and the danger signs.

- Signs lag about **6 weeks** behind symptoms (Campbell)
- Earliest: periarticular osteoporosis and capsular swelling
- The joint space is preserved until late arthritis: cartilage is spared
- Look for the crescent sign, the lateral pillar, subluxation and metaphyseal cysts

MRI sees the necrosis before the plain film.

- **Hot** during reossification and remodelling
- MRI has largely replaced it

### Bilateral Perthes or a Dysplasia
True bilateral Perthes is **asynchronous**: the hips are at different stages (Campbell).

| Feature | Perthes | MED (multiple epiphyseal dysplasia) |
|---|---|---|
| Hips | asymmetrical, different stages | **symmetrical**, same stage |
| Other epiphyses | normal | knees, ankles, shoulders involved |
| Acetabulum | late changes | **early** changes |
| Metaphyseal cysts | may occur | absent |
| Knee | normal | **double-layered patella** on the lateral view |
| Bone age | delayed | — |

- MED: both hips alike, with epiphyseal changes at the knee
[[FIG: Fig 5.68 · 5.7
- Get a **skeletal survey** and a wrist film for bone age
- Bilateral Perthes is usually more severe: mostly Herring B or C
- Spine involvement suggests **SED** (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia)
[[FIG: Fig 5.69 · 5.7
- No normal variant gives a fragmented proximal femoral epiphysis

#### Meyer Dysplasia
- Boys **under 4**, often bilateral: small, granular, late epiphyses (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 5.70 · 5.7
- No condensation, fracture, fragmentation or subluxation
- It resolves; do not treat it as Perthes

### Systemic Causes of Femoral Head Necrosis
Each gives an AVN or epiphyseal change with a cause, so it is not Perthes.

| Condition | Clue |
|---|---|
| **Hypothyroidism** | short child, delayed bone age, fragmented epiphyses on both sides |
